LESSON 68 OF 106·Web and Application Security Basics

File Uploads, Server-Side Requests and Input Validation

Three ways untrusted input reaches further than intended: a uploaded file that becomes something else, a URL the server fetches on a caller's behalf, and validation that checks the wrong property.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

Input validation, file handling and server-side requests are grouped together because they share one root cause: the application lets untrusted input decide what the server does next.

  1. Verification: Store uploads outside the web root, and serve them with a neutral content type and a content disposition of attachment.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.
  3. Resilience: Invalid requests fail closed and emit structured security telemetry.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Validation has to happen on the server, on the parsed value, not only in the browser form.
  • A file upload is dangerous because the filename, the declared type and the actual content can all differ.
  • If uploaded files are served from the same origin as the application, a crafted file can run as script against your own users.
  • Server-side request forgery happens when a URL from a user decides where the server connects, which reaches things the user cannot.
  • Server-side request forgery is especially useful against cloud metadata services, which return credentials to whoever asks.

The background

  • Client-side validation was long treated as validation, and it protected nothing once the request was sent directly.
  • Web shells arrived through file uploads, and the fix was separating storage from execution.
  • Server-side request forgery was named once cloud metadata services made it valuable, and it remains a default-credential route.
  • Modern frameworks do more validation by default, which helps only where teams use the built-in mechanism.

Real-world examples

  • An upload directory inside the web root means a crafted HTML or SVG file executes in the site origin.
  • A preview feature that fetches a user-supplied URL can be aimed at an internal metadata endpoint and return credentials.
  • A file-type check based on the extension or the client-declared content type is defeated trivially.

What to look for

  • Check where uploaded files are stored and whether they are served with a content type that cannot execute.
  • Check whether validation happens server-side, on the value after parsing.
  • Check every feature that takes a URL and fetches it, and see whether the destination is restricted.
  • Check whether the fetch follows redirects, since a redirect can bypass an allow-list.

Key takeaways

  • Store uploads outside the web root, and serve them with a neutral content type and a content disposition of attachment.
  • Validate on the server against the actual content, not the filename or the declared type.
  • If the server must render a user file, sanitise it rather than trusting the content.
  • For server-side requests, allow-list destinations, resolve the address, and re-check after every redirect.
  • Block access to instance metadata endpoints from application workloads at the network layer.
